newsitem.title: USA: Democrats claim "inconsistencies" in Barbour story.
newsitem.headline: Democrats claim "inconsistencies" in Barbour story.

text.p: Haley Barbour, the former head of the Republican National Committee, sought a $2.1 million loan from a Hong Kong businessman in 1994 to help finance a final push to claim a Republican majority in Congress, a prominent Utah Republican testified on Friday.
The sworn statements of Richard Richards before the Senate panel investigating how foreign money flowed to U.S. political parties contradicted earlier testimony from Barbour.

Richards said that Barbour asked him to solicit the loan from a wealthy Hong Kong entrepreneur in a complicated arrangement involving the National Policy Forum, a think-tank largely funded by the Republican Party until it was disbanded.

In a telephone conversation with Richards in August 1994, Barbour said the funds were needed "to assist in the election of 60 potential new Republican congressmen," Richards said under questioning by Democratic members of the panel.
"If we had thought they were flush with money, we probably would not have entered into discussions with them," Richards said, referring to his client, Ambrous Young of Hong Kong.
Young, who renounced his U.S. citizenship in 1993, was eager to curry favour with the Republican Party but did not expect to be repaid with any political favours, Richards said.
Richards' version of the $2.1 million transaction differed from Barbour's own testimony on Thursday.

In his appearance before the Senate Governmental Affairs committee, Barbour said no foreign money was illegally funnelled into Republican campaigns in 1994. He also testified that he was unaware that a Hong Kong developer was the source of the $2.1 million loan until recently.

Democratic members of the panel have tried to show that the loan was orchestrated through the National Policy Forum as a front for the Republican Party and that the party used most of the money for a dozen state campaigns to help it win control of Congress for the first time in 40 years.
After months of prodding by Richards, a Utah attorney, the forum eventually repaid only about $750,000 of the loan to Young in 1996. The organisation defaulted on the rest.
Richards served as chairman of the Republican National Committee from 1981-1983, the early years of the Reagan administration.
Sen. Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican who heads the panel, acknowledged he had "some problems" with Barbour's account of the transaction.
But he said any allegations of misconduct by Barbour paled in comparison to allegations about President Bill Clinton's 1996 re-election campaign contributions.

Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, the senior Democrat on the panel, stopped short of accusing Barbour of perjury but said he found the contradictions troubling. "There are some very, very serious inconsistencies," he said.
Both Glenn and Thompson urged members of the panel to take a bipartisan approach to campaign finance irregularities by both parties and to craft legislation to reform the system.

After the hearing adjourned, Republican aides on the panel said investigators would decide by early next week whether to subpoena the White House for certain campaign-related documents. Other subpoenas could be forthcoming as the committee continues trying to trace foreign contributions to the Clinton campaign, they said.

At the heart of the investigation is Asian-American John Huang, who worked in the Clinton administration at the Commerce Department and later solicited millions of dollars in illegal contributions from Asian business interests.
